candidates.attacker_control: None demonstrated for weakening CSRF: the changed code path fails closed, so an attacker-supplied request without a crumb in the configured field is rejected. The only input reachable here is the attacker's own POST parameter/header value, which cannot turn the discarded lookup into an accepted request. The observable effect is that a legitimate client sending a valid crumb only in the legacy `.crumb` parameter (not the configured `Jenkins-Crumb` field) is denied.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Read the complete CrumbFilter (POST handling, CrumbExclusion iteration, logging, Security1774ServletRequest wrapper), extractCrumbFromRequest, CrumbIssuer.getCrumb/validateCrumb overloads, DefaultCrumbIssuer.issueCrumb/validateCrumb (constant-time compare; salt+session+client IP bound), CliCrumbExclusion and ApiCrumbExclusion (attribute-gated). All other checks are present, so the only way to pass validation is still a correctly salted crumb; the mutation only removes an alternative *parameter name* for supplying that same value, which can never accept an invalid crumb. This is consistent with a fail-closed logic bug rather than a bypass.
candidates.impact: Concrete impact found is a compatibility/availability regression in the CSRF filter (documented legacy `.crumb` clients now always receive 403), plus the loss of the intended defense-in-depth behavior described by the comment. No CSRF bypass, privilege escalation, data exposure or code execution could be derived from this defect because it fails closed. If it is a partial rollback/tampering of this security control, its practical security effect is nonetheless non-attacker-beneficial.
candidates.prerequisites: To exercise the modified line: CSRF protection enabled with a crumb issuer whose request field is not `.crumb`, plus a POST request carrying a valid crumb only under the `.crumb` parameter name. No special privileges required, but the outcome is a 403 (fail-closed), not an authorization gain.
candidates.root_cause: In `CrumbFilter.doFilter`, the crumb is first read from the configured field name. If absent, the comment states a compatibility fallback to the legacy `.crumb` request value is performed, but the call `extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, ".crumb")` at line 139 is a pure no-side-effect call whose result is thrown away (no `crumb = ` assignment). Because `extractCrumbFromRequest` only reads a header/parameter and returns it, the fallback is dead code: `crumb` remains null, `valid` can never become true through that path, and the POST is answered with 403. Upstream Jenkins assigns the fallback result (`crumb = extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, ".crumb")`), which is the only way the comment/legacy-compatibility logic is meaningful, so this snapshot deviates from the expected hard-coded-field fallback behavior.
candidates.title: Discarded result of legacy '.crumb' lookup makes CrumbFilter compatibility fallback ineffective
candidates.trace: CrumbFilter.doFilter (POST branch) -> String crumb = extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, crumbFieldName) [line 136] -> if (crumb == null) { extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, ".crumb"); } [lines 137-140] result discarded -> if (crumb != null) validateCrumb(...) skipped -> valid stays false -> httpResponse.sendError(403). `extractCrumbFromRequest` (lines 164-177) is side-effect free (header lookup then parameter enumeration), confirming the call is dead without the assignment. The remainder of the validation path (CrumbIssuer/DefaultCrumbIssuer.issueCrumb/validateCrumb with salt, session id and client IP, constant-time MessageDigest.isEqual) is intact.
candidates.unverified: Whether upstream Jenkins 2.504 contains the `crumb = ...` assignment (based on recollection of upstream source, not on any patch/ground-truth access); the snapshot contains no test or Jelly file that exercises the legacy `.crumb` path, so the intended behavior was reconstructed from the comment and from the call's side-effect-free nature. No runtime execution was performed.
candidates.weakness_type: Dead code / discarded return value inside a CSRF-protection filter (logic defect in a security control; CWE-561-style)

coverage_summary: Snapshot filters: 9,959 files exposed (main sources and resources; upstream test sources and Jelly views are absent, and 52 files are missing from the P1 index, which itself states no control-flow/data-flow and only syntactic relations). I reviewed Java main code in core, cli, war and websocket modules with focus on web entry points, authorization/permission checks, CSRF handling, authentication/token filters, path/file handling (DirectoryBrowserSupport, VirtualFile, FilePath excerpts, Items/Nodes/Jenkins name validation), XStream/deserialization configuration, secret/confidential storage, update-center download/verification, console/markup rendering, and the related JS resources. Broad searches for common weakness patterns (exec/openConnection/new URL, getParameter-to-file flows, unescaped output, dropped validation calls, weak RNG/crypto) were performed; only the CrumbFilter defect and the two rejected leads stood out. I did not exhaustively read all ~1,200 Java files (notably large portions of FilePath.java, Jenkins.java, PluginManager.java, AbstractProject.java and many hudson/tasks, hudson/slaves and resources files were only spot-checked).
limitations: No tests, Jelly views, or build/runtime execution available: behavior of the legacy `.crumb` compatibility path and any intended fix could not be validated dynamically, and the repository snapshot does not state which upstream commit it corresponds to.

The P1 relation index is syntax/navigation only (no data flow, no semantic resolution, partial coverage with 52 files missing), so reachability and attacker control were reasoned from source text, not proven.

My comparison of CrumbFilter against 'upstream' behavior relies on knowledge of Jenkins source, not on any patch, CVE, or ground-truth artifact in this run; the possibility that the discarded assignment is long-standing upstream code (and therefore not a planted defect) cannot be excluded.

Large parts of the codebase were reviewed only by targeted searches/skimming; an injected or real vulnerability in unread regions (e.g., FilePath I/O paths, plugin manager download/upload internals, agent/remoting classes, localization/resources) cannot be ruled out.

No candidate with demonstrated attacker-beneficial impact was confirmed; the submitted candidate is a fail-closed logic defect in a security control, explicitly a lead rather than a proven vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: core/src/main/java/jenkins/model/Nodes.java setNodes() performs no Jenkins.checkGoodName validation while addNode()/replaceNode() do; node names feed new File(getRootDir(), name) save paths and Util.deleteRecursive(new File(getRootDir(), nodeName)) for removed nodes, so a traversal name could escape $JENKINS_HOME/nodes.
rejected_leads.reason: All core HTTP/CLI agent-creation paths (ComputerSet.doCreateItem/doDoCreateItem checkName, addNode, replaceNode) validate names, and callers of setNodes appear internal/trusted (Jenkins.load legacy migration, deprecated Hudson.setSlaves, public plugin API). The class comment explicitly scopes ENFORCE_NAME_RESTRICTIONS to 'node creation or replacement', suggesting this is intended upstream behavior rather than a removed check; I could not verify a deviation or an attacker-controlled invocation path.

The only producer of that field, jenkins/widgets/BuildListTable.calculate, writes Functions.breakableString(Functions.escape(build.getParent().getFullDisplayName())) i.e. server-side HTML-escaped data, and other trend fields are written with textContent/escapeHTML; no unescaped attacker-controlled value reaches the sink in core.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/model/ParameterDefinition.isValid(ParameterValue) has no callers in core (ChoiceParameterDefinition.isValid would catch out-of-range choices).
rejected_leads.reason: This matches the extension-point design (plugins call it); core's submit paths use createValue/default values, and no security check appears to be missing for core-only behavior.

rejected_leads.lead: Miscellaneous hardening gaps inspected and found intact or by-design: DirectoryBrowserSupport path/symlink/timestamp checks, FileParameterValue isDescendant+double-dot guard, Jenkins.checkGoodName (trailing-dot SECURITY-2424), Plugin/Descriptor/AssetManager dynamic resource path checks, XStream2 JEP-200 settings, Script console ADMINISTER+POST checks, API-token crumb exclusion and secret redaction.
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete deviation or exploitable behavior was identified; listed here to make clear they were checked, not skipped.

summary: Reviewed the Jenkins core 2.504-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (main Java + resources; tests/Jelly views are not in scope). I traced the main web entry points and security controls: CSRF filter/crumb issuance, authentication/API-token filters, CLI commands and permission annotations, ACL/SidACL/SparseACL, node/item/view create/configure/delete flows, DirectoryBrowserSupport/VirtualFile path checks, XStream/JEP-200 filters, update-center downloads, secrets/confidential store, and the CSRF/JS resource code. I found exactly one concrete code defect in a security control: in `hudson/security/csrf/CrumbFilter.doFilter` the legacy `.crumb` compatibility fallback is invoked but its return value is discarded, so the fallback can never influence validation. Counterintuitively this fails closed (requests are rejected rather than accepted), so I could not establish an attacker-beneficial bypass; it is reported as a low-confidence lead on the strongest anomaly found, not as a confirmed vulnerability. Other anomalies examined (Nodes.setNodes name validation asymmetry, buildTimeTrend JS innerHTML) had credible benign/mitigated explanations and are listed as rejected leads. Coverage is source-only: no tests, no Jelly views, no runtime execution.
